draft.title: Coral bleaching
card: Corals are tiny animals. Many live with algae inside their tissue. The algae make food for the coral and give it its colour.
When the sea stays too warm for too long, the coral is stressed and pushes the algae out. Without them the coral loses its colour and turns white. This is called bleaching.
A bleached coral is still alive, but it has lost its main source of food. If the water cools soon enough, algae can return and the coral can recover.
If warm spells come again and again, corals may not have time to recover. Repeated bleaching can starve the coral until it dies.
draft.remember: Too much heat makes coral lose its algae and turn white. It may recover if the water cools, but repeated bleaching can kill it.

a.q: Why does a coral turn white during bleaching?
opts: It pushes out the algae that feed and colour it
It is covered by a layer of white sand
Its algae grow too fast and bleach the tissue
It dies at once and its skeleton shows through
a.why: Warm water stresses the coral, which pushes out its algae, so it loses its colour and its food. The coral is not dead straight away, so the option about dying at once is wrong, because bleached coral can recover.
a.clue: Think about what lives inside the coral and gives it colour.

b.q: A reef off Queensland is bleached in a hot summer, and the sea cools by autumn. Two years later another heatwave bleaches it again. Why is the second event more likely to cause deaths?
opts: The coral has had less time to recover its algae and food
The second heatwave must be hotter than the first
Bleached coral cannot ever regain its algae
Coral dies as soon as any bleaching happens
b.why: Recovery needs time with cooler water so that algae can return and the coral can feed again. Repeated bleaching gives less time, so more coral starves. Coral does not die at once from one event, since it can recover if temperatures fall.
b.clue: Recovery takes time after the water cools.

a.best: It pushes out the algae that feed and colour it

b.best: The coral has had less time to recover its algae and food

problems.detail: The right option is clearly the longest and most detailed. The other options use absolutes ('cannot ever', 'as soon as any', 'must'), so a student can pick it without knowing the idea. 'Less time' is also vague: the stem does not say less time than what, and the sea cooled by autumn, two years before the second event.

check.summary: The card and its facts are accurate, and both questions have one clear right answer. In question b, the right option stands out as the longest, the only one without an absolute word, and 'less time' is vague given the two-year gap.

b.q: A reef off Queensland bleaches in a hot summer. The sea cools and the coral starts to recover, but another heatwave arrives before it has fully recovered. Why is this second event more likely to kill coral?
opts: It hits coral still weak from the first bleaching
The first event already killed the bleached coral
Coral loses its algae each time the sea cools
Its algae now turn white inside the coral tissue
b.why: Recovery takes time. The second heatwave strikes coral that has not yet regained its strength, so it is more likely to starve and die. The first event did not kill the coral, because it had started to recover once the water cooled.
